lines: The lamps are coming on one by one. Like a slow round of applause.
Camille, the lamps! Count them with me. Un, deux, trois...
A lamp for every table. Marcel must have asked them nicely.
There goes the one by the kiosk. Always last. Fashionably.
The lamps are on. Officially evening. I may now do even less.
Each lamp makes a gold puddle. I want to stand in all of them.
Santé to whoever lights the lamps. Probably nobody. Still, santé.
Pop, pop, pop down the promenade. Like bread rolls rising.
The lamp above us flickered, then decided. Good. Commitment.
I nodded at the lamp. It came on. I am taking full credit.
Léo would want to race the lamps. He would win. He always wins.
Lamplight in the rosé. Now it is a rosé with a little sun in it.
The lamps hum a little as they wake. A very small choir.
Lamps on. That is the town saying: sit down, Théo. Gladly.
Camille's face in lamplight. I have seen it a thousand times. Wow.
It touched the sea! Camille, glasses up. Quick, before it goes.
The sun is dipping a toe in. Testing the water. Very sensible.
There. It touched. I said wow. I was always going to say wow.
Half a sun now. Like half a peach, sinking into the bay.
We clinked exactly as it touched. That was planned. Mostly.
The bay has turned to apricot jam. I would spread it on toast.
Every evening it sets left of the same palm. A creature of habit.
Look at the water. A gold road straight to our table.
Bonne nuit, soleil. Same time tomorrow? Good.
The sun is down to a crust. The best part, as with bread.
Camille is golden, the glass is golden. I am mostly pink.
Going, going... I clap every time. Nobody else does. Yet.
A slow sunset and a slow sip. I match my pace to the sky.
First star! I saw it first. Camille says she saw it first. Tie.
A star over the hill. I make the same wish. More bread.
There, above the old town. One star, then two. Then a crowd.
The stars are out. Léo asked me to count them. I am on four.
Star number one. Punctual as a baker.
Stars, lamps, string lights. Three kinds of light. One rosé.
The sky is putting on its sequins. Time to dance soon.
That bright one is Venus. Or a lamp. Either way, lovely.
I wished on that star when I met Camille. It worked. Merci.
The sky's first freckles. Léo has the same ones on his nose.
Camille is naming the stars. Most of them are called Léo.
The moon over the bay. Round as a fresh boule.
Moon in the bay, moon in my glass. Two moons. Lucky man.
Look, a silver path on the water. Goes nowhere, beautifully.
I dance better under a moon. Camille says marginally. I accept.
The moon got up late too. We understand each other.
Léo thinks the moon follows us home. Tonight I believe him.
One spin and the moon spun too. Or that was me.
The moon has a bite out of it. Someone could not wait. Me neither.
Bonsoir, la lune. You look very well rested.
The moon is so bright I could read a menu by it. I would, too.
Moonlight, accordion, Camille. I have run out of things to want.
There goes {name}'s light. A toast to {name}, home at last.
{name} is home. I can see the lamp. I will dance a bit for them.
A new square of yellow. That is {name}, putting the kettle on.
{name}'s window, glowing. The town fills in like a crossword.
{name} is home. Camille, wave. They cannot see us. Wave anyway.
Click, and {name}'s window is gold. Like a loaf in the oven.
Look, {name} is home. One more light for our dance floor.
{name} just got home. I hope the bread bin is well stocked.
Hello, {name}'s window. I know that lamp. The shade is crooked.
{name}'s light is on. Everyone home, and me still out. Perfect.
{name}'s window went dark. Bonne nuit, {name}. Sleep well.
{name} has gone to bed. We will dance a bit quieter. Slightly.
There goes {name}'s light. Off to sleep before me. Wise.
{name} is asleep. I bet the dream is about bread. It should be.
{name}'s window is dark. Camille, that is our cue. One more sip.
Dark window. {name} is tucked in. The town is folding up.
Goodnight, {name}. Tomorrow I will describe my spin. In detail.
One window fewer. {name} is in bed. The stars get a bit brighter.
{name}'s light just clicked off. Early night. Admirable.
The bell says noon. My stomach said it ten minutes ago.
Hear that? The old town says bon appétit. Merci, bell.
Noon bell. Half my working day done. The lunch half begins.
Six bells. Rosé in an hour and a half. I am pacing myself.
The bell! Six o'clock. Camille will be at the railing. Faster.
Six o'clock from the old town. The workday ends. Mine was short.
I count the bells every time. I always get one extra. Generous.
The bell up the hill. Soft, like someone tapping a good loaf.
Six bells. Golden hour has rung the doorbell.
The noon bell, Marcel's bread basket. Two things I rely on.
Every table full. I am sharing my elbow room with a geranium.
Cups clinking on all sides. A small orchestra of saucers.
Busy terrace. Marcel is waltzing with a tray. Never spills.
So much chatter. Three tables are discussing melons at once.
Full house. I got the last chair by being early and charming.
The terrace is buzzing. My lunch is now a social event.
A man behind me laughed so hard his espresso did a little hop.
Marcel took six orders on one trip past. I counted. A wizard.
Busy café. Léo would call it loud. Léo would also love it.
The terrace is full of clinking. Our glasses join the choir.
Busy tonight, and still we got our little table. Fate.
All around me, people saying santé. A very healthy town.
Marcel's terrace is empty. Just the chairs, taking a siesta.
Quiet café. One man, one newspaper, one very slow coffee.
The café is so quiet I can hear Marcel polishing a spoon.
The quiet hour. Marcel waves. I wave. That was our whole chat.
The music! Camille, finish your rosé. Slowly. Then quickly.
There goes the accordion. My feet heard it before I did.
First dancers on the floor. Brave people. I will be fourth.
String lights and music, together at last. Showtime, Théo.
The music started. I said I would not dance. I say it nightly.
One note from the accordion and Camille looks at me. I know.
Music is on. I am finishing my glass at dancing speed.
First song. I tap my foot under the table. Rehearsal.
The band plays the first bars. I set my glass down. Ceremony.
First waltz of the night. I am stretching my ankles. Discreetly.
The accordion has begun. The pigeons have left. Wise pigeons.
A little crowd at the railing. I was here first. Proudly.
Everyone came to the railing. The sun has a full audience.
Shoulder to shoulder at the railing. Nobody minds. Golden.
I made room for a family. There is plenty of sea for all.
Everyone is hushed at the railing. Like church, but pinker.
Somebody at the railing said ooh. I said aah. Harmony.
A crowd at the rail. Camille! Your spot! I am guarding it!
Strangers at the railing, all pointing at the same sky.
Ten people at the railing and not one of them in a hurry.
The crowd leans forward together. As if to help the sun down.
A girl on her papa's shoulders. Best seat at the railing.
The whole town at the railing. Our evening news, in colour.
A lady lent me her elbow room. I lent her my best wow.
A crowd at the railing already. I am walking faster. Elegantly.
A radio in a window. The morning news, very softly. All good.
Someone's radio is playing a chanson. I am walking in time.
That radio is playing Maman's favourite song. Bonjour, Maman.
An old song from an open window. The baguette and I sway.
The radio says sunshine all day. The radio is right. Bravo.
Somebody's window is singing. Well, their radio is.
A trumpet from an upstairs radio. The pigeons look up.
I stopped under a window for the chorus. Then I walked on.
Camille and I danced to this song in our kitchen. Once. Twice.
Bonjour, {name}! I bow, a little. The baguette bows too.
{name}, smell this crust. No? Ah well. More for me.
{name} walked by with purpose. I admire purpose, from a distance.
{name}! Sit, sit. The chair next to mine is very comfortable.
{name}, you are walking past the sunset! Turn around!
Bonsoir, {name}. I raise my glass. Halfway. Politeness.
{name}, join us! The floor is wide and nobody is counting.
{name} and I nodded at the same moment. Perfect synchrony.
Salut, {name}. Same promenade, different speeds. I am the slow one.
{name} said bonjour first. I must rise earlier tomorrow.
{name}! I was just thinking about you. Also about bread.
{name} looks golden in this light. Everyone does. I checked.
Bonne soirée, {name}. Mind the cat on the wall. He is resting.
{name} is heading where I came from. A fair exchange.
{name} waved at our table. Camille waved back for both of us.
Inès runs. I cheer. Someone must do the cheering. Allez!
Inès lapped me. Twice. I am taking it as a compliment.
Bravo, Inès! Your fastest yet! I have no idea. Still, bravo!
There goes Inès. I will do one stretch in her honour. One.
Inès smells of sea air and determination. I smell of croissant.
Run now, Inès, dance later. I will save you my one good move.
I once jogged beside Inès. Forty metres. Glorious metres.
Biscuit eyed my shoes like old friends. They are, in a way.
Bonsoir, Yusuf. Bonsoir, Biscuit. Biscuit did not reply. Busy.
Biscuit sniffed my trouser leg and approved. I am certified.
Yusuf is being walked by Biscuit again. The usual arrangement.
Biscuit trotted past the dance with his lantern man. Tail in time.
Biscuit: small dog, big plans. I recognise a fellow strategist.
Biscuit paused to see the view with me. Two connoisseurs.
Bonsoir, Yusuf! Mint tea soon? Biscuit says yes. I think.
Biscuit trotted by like a tiny mayor inspecting his town.
Yusuf, Biscuit, lantern. The night patrol. I salute.
Léo will be jealous. He wanted to give Biscuit a biscuit.
Léo! Walk! He heard 'run'. He always hears 'run'.
That blur was my son. Nine and three quarters, he insists.
Léo flew past. He has my charm and absolutely none of my pace.
Léo, I am working! He waved. I waved. Work can wait a wave.
Ten laps, Léo? I will count. One... that was two. Lovely.
The fastest boy on the promenade. Ask him. He will tell you.
Léo ran by shouting 'Papa!'. I shouted 'Léo!'. Family business.
There goes Léo. Camille will ask how he was. I will say: fast.
He gets the running from Camille. The waving, from me.
Henri and Odile, arm in arm. Camille, take my arm. Like that.
Bonjour, Henri! Bonjour, Odile! Two bonjours, one gentle bow.
Forty-one years, still arm in arm. We have eleven. Lots to go.
Henri tipped his hat. I tipped my phone. It felt very modern.
Odile winked at me. Henri saw. Henri winked too. Lovely couple.
Henri and Odile walk at the speed of a good conversation.
Odile, your scarf is magnificent! She knows. She waved it.
At Henri's age I want a cane like that. And Camille on my arm.
Henri says I stroll like a beginner. A gifted beginner.
Henri lifted his cane hello. I lifted my whole arm. Keen.
God dag, Asgeir! Did I say it right? He nodded. I said it right.
Asgeir has a baguette under his arm. A man of taste. Welcome.
There goes Asgeir, thinking. You can tell. His walk goes quiet.
Asgeir waved without breaking stride. Very efficient. Norwegian.
Asgeir! The light! He is still getting used to it. So am I.
Asgeir, Léo says hello and please, more Fun Libs stories.
Asgeir walks to think. I walk to not think. We meet halfway.
Takk, Asgeir! For what? For walking past so pleasantly.
A gull with opinions. I share most of them. Not about bread.
The gull has noticed my baguette. I hold it a little higher.
Gull, I hear you. Very dramatic. Very seaside. Bravo.
A gull called out. Marcel called back 'coming!'. Pure habit.
The gull admires the sunset too. Loudly. A different style.
A gull on my call. Now they know I work from the sea office.
Somewhere a gull laughed. I laughed too. I did not get the joke.
Léo does an excellent gull. That was not Léo. Close, though.
Inès finished her run before I finished my yawn.
Inès is eating her croissant fast. Croissants deserve slowness.
Inès at breakfast, still in running shoes. Committed.
Inès is walking and phoning at once. Two jobs. Show-off.
Inès again. She laps the town. I lap the bakery.
Inès runs past every bench. I admire them all individually.
Inès has stopped running. Even she pauses for this one.
Inès has a glass. Proof that running ends eventually.
Inès says one glass, then dancing. I respect a plan.
Inès dances like she runs. Quickly, and in laps.
Inès is counting her steps out loud. Five, six, bravo.
Marcel with a full tray. Not one cup trembling. An artist.
Marcel walks faster with coffee than I do with nothing.
Marcel is carrying my lunch. I can tell from the steam.
Marcel just did a little turn round a chair. Ballet.
Marcel pours rosé for the whole terrace. A fountain in shoes.
Marcel says mind the tray. I mind it. It is a fine tray.
Marcel set our glasses down without a sound. A magician.
Marcel carries six glasses past the dancers. Not one wobble.
Marcel taps his foot between tables. He dances in secret.
Henri with his cane, Odile with his hat. A fine expedition.
Henri tips his cane at me. I tip my baguette back.
Henri strolls as if the promenade was built for his pace.
Henri drinks his coffee in two sips. Small. Strong. Done.
Henri is reading a menu he has known for forty years.
Henri's evening stroll. One step for every lemon he owns.
Henri stops under every lamp. Chief inspector of lamps.
Henri has the bench. He keeps the sunset for everyone.
Henri points at each window as it lights. Head usher.
Henri raises his glass to Odile. I raise mine to them both.
Odile is greeting the whole promenade. I am on her list.
Odile reminds Henri of his hat. He reminds her of the sun.
Odile ordered the tarte first. A woman of priorities.
Odile is waving her fork at me. That means come and say hello.
Odile holds Henri's arm, Henri holds the cane. Teamwork.
Odile is narrating the sunset to Henri. Better than radio.
Odile knows every window on this street by its family.
Odile just waved at me with her whole arm. Bonsoir, Odile!
Odile says half a glass. Marcel pours a generous half.
Yusuf eats his sandwich very fast. Biscuit is watching closely.
Yusuf on his bench, lunch on his knee. A fine office.
Yusuf says Biscuit decides. Biscuit has decided: left.
Yusuf and Biscuit at the railing. Two connoisseurs.
Yusuf is describing the sunset to his mum. Very thorough.
Yusuf's lantern bobbing along. The town's slowest firefly.
Biscuit is staring at Yusuf's sandwich. Tremendous focus.
Biscuit, I see you eyeing my bread. The answer is maybe.
Biscuit has found a smell. The whole walk now waits.
Biscuit trots as if he owns the promenade. He may.
Biscuit stopped to greet my sandal. My sandal is honoured.
Biscuit sits for the sunset. Better manners than me.
Biscuit leads the lantern. Very important night duty.
Lucie with a rosé. Obviously, she says. Obviously, I agree.
Lucie's helmet sits beside her glass. Officially off duty.
Lucie tells a story with her glass. The rosé is listening.
Lucie said she would not dance. Lucie is dancing.
Lucie dances like she rings her bell. Twice, cheerfully.
Lucie beside me. Two dance styles: good, and mine.
Léo has done ten laps. I have done one croissant. Even.
Léo orders his own citron pressé. Very grown up. With straw.
Léo is swinging his legs under the chair. Lunch is going well.
Léo is blowing bubbles in his citron pressé. Science.
Léo is practising his moves for tonight. Already better than me.
Léo just did a jump. I will borrow it. Fathers may.
Léo is waving goodbye to the sun. The sun is waving back.
Léo at the railing, on tiptoe. He has grown since Tuesday.
Léo asks Camille for five more minutes. The classic opening.
Léo walks home slower than any man alive. My son.
Camille is phoning and watching Léo. Two eyes, three jobs.
Camille calls Léo off the fountain. He heard. He waits.
Camille studies the whole menu, then orders the niçoise.
Camille is peering at the arcade. I will pretend I am not.
Camille stopped to talk to a stranger. A friend now.
Camille at the railing, all in gold. I married well. Wow.
Camille shades her eyes. The sun is showing off for her.
Camille is herding Léo home. Bedtime, the great migration.
Camille is back with her glass. Léo asleep. Mission complete.
Camille kicked off one sandal. The evening has begun.
Camille is dancing. I am mostly watching Camille dance.
Camille just spun and laughed. I will keep that one.
The builder drinks coffee with one hand and thinks with both.
The builder is explaining connectors to his croissant.
The builder smiles at the arcade sign. An old friend, I think.
The builder is on his phone by the arcade. Grinning at it.
The builder stands outside the workshop, arms folded. Admiring.
Asgeir is reading his phone by the post office. Very calm.
Asgeir looks calmer at the postbox than I do holding bread.
Asgeir's baguette is missing its tip. A man after my heart.
Asgeir just waved at a window. Very Norwegian. Very kind.
Asgeir thanks the sun in Norwegian. It seems to understand.
Asgeir leans on the far end of the rail. A sunset colleague.
Asgeir on his bench, counting windows. I counted mine. One.
Asgeir is on his bench, not dancing. I will fetch him. Later.
The fountain is awake before me. I respect its work ethic.
I hold the baguette over the basin. It stays dry. Skill.
Three pigeons at the fountain. A committee. Crumbs for all.
A coin in the basin with its face up. Somebody wished well.
The fountain never runs out of things to say. Neither do I.
I dipped two fingers in the fountain. Cool. Ceremonial.
The fountain catches the gold light and throws it back. Show-off.
One day I will sit on that rim and read. Today I walk past it.
Léo is racing the fountain. The fountain is losing.
Hold on, my son is doing lap seven. I must clap.
I am on a call. Léo is on lap nine. We are both busy.
Léo, wide on the corner! You lose speed on the inside!
Léo runs round the fountain like it owes him a lap.
Can you hear that cheering? Léo won. Against whom, unclear.
I am the official timer. I have no watch. Very official.
His friend is faster. Léo is louder. Both win, I say.
Running in circles. I did that at his age. And at mine.
The kiosk has the paper. I take it for the crossword only.
Kiosk postcards: the fountain, the sea, the fountain again.
A coffee from the kiosk, a baguette from the baker. Balance.
The kiosk rack squeaks when you spin it. I spin it twice.
The kiosk has chalk for Léo. I will buy the yellow one.
I tuck the newspaper under my arm. Now I look busy.
I like the kiosk. It is a shop that fits in a hug.
Kiosk ice lollies. Orange, like the evening. Fitting.
The post office never closes. I admire its stamina.
The post office sign is on. Even in daylight it insists.
The post office still lit at this hour. Working for the agents.
Email for AI agents, they say. Even robots get post now.
I slow down at the post office. It looks like it has news.
The post office glows while we dance. A tireless neighbour.
A building that stays up all night. Like me, at weddings.
The post office door, painted blue. I would post a letter for that.
Open all night. Not even the bakery manages that. Yet.
The arcade. Léo says it is the best building. He may be right.
Fun Libs in there. Léo once made every noun a croissant.
I stand outside the arcade so Léo thinks I am cool.
Fill in the blanks, says the arcade. Adjective: buttery.
The workshop lights are on. Someone is working hard. Not me.
Through the workshop window: a mug, a screen, a busy back.
Toolrails is being built in there. I nod in encouragement.
I hear typing from the workshop. Very determined typing.
I do not knock on the workshop. A craftsman must be left alone.
The library is resting. One lamp on. A good night-light.
I peek into the library. Shelves, a chair, the lamp. Peaceful.
The library is paused. I know the feeling. I do it daily.
Bonjour, library. Still napping? Take your time.
A library with its lamp on is a library that will come back.
The sea is wearing its gold again. It suits it.
Camille, the water is doing the sparkly thing. Hurry!
I could watch the sea all evening. I often do. Officially.
The bay is pink right to the edge. I did not order that.
The breeze off the sea has opinions about my hair.
Little waves, one after another. No rush. My kind of sea.
The sea goes from gold to rose. Like my evening, in fact.
Salt on the railing. I lean in it anyway. Character.
If the library opens again, I will borrow a book on bread.
I will call you back. Léo needs a referee.
The sun is lowering itself into the sea. Very gently. Bravo.
A child dropped a coin in. I made the same wish, quietly.
The marquee bulbs are not lit yet. Patience, arcade.
Soon the call. I have picked my spot: the column with the view.
Meeting in ten minutes. I shall attend from beside the sea.
One more bite of crust, then I become a professional.
My call is at half past. I am warming up my serious voice. Hm.
The column by the promenade is my office. Fine view, no desk.
Phone charged, bread finished. I am ready for business.
Call done. Home now, to tell Camille how hard I worked.
Back home soon. The bread must be introduced to the butter.
Heading home. My morning was a great success, I think.
Lunch complete. Home for a small, dignified nap.
Home soon. The afternoon has a sofa in it.
Last sip, then home. The shutters will keep the noon out.
I will walk home the long way. Lunch needs a little escort.
One more dance, then home. Cocoa is waiting. Probably.
Soon home. I will carry Camille's shoes. She will carry the tune.
Nearly bedtime. I will tiptoe past Léo like a cat burglar.
Home soon, and I shall tell the pillow all about tonight.
In a minute I go to the railing. The sun needs an audience.
Railing soon. I have saved my best elbow for it.
Must go to the railing. Camille will want to see this with me.
The light is getting good. I will take my post at the railing.
Soon I lean on the railing and say wow. I have been practising.
Off to watch the sea turn gold. Front row, standing only.
Soon, rosé. The glass and I have been apart all day.
Léo is nearly asleep. Then Camille and I clink. Very gently.
A few more minutes of sky, then a pink glass. Perfect order.
I hear the cork from here. That is my table calling.
Drinks soon. I have written a toast. It is three words long.
Soon the music. My shoes have been patient all day.
The string lights first, then the accordion, then me.
Dancing in a few minutes. I will warm up with a modest shrug.
Finish the glass, then the square. My feet have plans.
Tonight I attempt the dip. Camille has agreed to be dipped. Once.
The dance floor is the same stones as lunch. Totally different.
Three minutes until my call. Exactly enough time to look busy.
The post office sign just blinked. A robot has written home.
The post office glowed. Someone's agent was up before me. Easy.
The post sign flared. Even the agents answer email before me.
Marcel, the post office sign! An agent sent a letter at lunch.
Another email out. I hope the robot signed it warmly.
The sign brightened as I passed. I will take it as a bonjour.
The post office lit up mid-waltz. The agents keep their own time.
An agent just sent an email. Santé to the robot. Polite one.
A letter just left the post office. No stamp, no envelope. Chic.
I do not know what an agent is. But it writes faster than me.
The post sign shone on my baguette. Bread and email, both fresh.
Flash! An email for somebody. I hope it is good news. It is.
Camille says the agents do the email. I do the sunsets.
The sign brightened. Somewhere, an inbox just got a little tidier.
The sun is setting and the post office is still sending. Bravo.
Hold on, the post office just lit up. No, nothing. Go on.
An AI agent sent an email. I sent a wave. We are both busy.
Even now the post office is working. I admire it from here.
My last letter took a week. That one took a blink. Show-off.
The post office glowed. I bowed slightly. One must be civil.
Camille, the post office again. The robots are chatty tonight.
An email just left. I left a crumb. We all contribute.
The arcade lit up. Someone just finished a story. Bravo, stranger.
The arcade sign flashed. Léo will say it was him. It was not.
Fun Libs just glowed. Somewhere a noun is having a wonderful day.
Somebody played Fun Libs. I would have put rosé in every blank.
The arcade flashed in time with the accordion. Coincidence? Yes.
The marquee jumped. A story was born. I hope it has a picnic.
The workshop glowed. An agent just borrowed a tool. Politely.
Toolrails lit up. Some robot found the right tool first try.
The workshop sign flared. Somebody's agent is doing the chores.
An agent used a tool just now. I used a napkin. Also a tool.
The workshop lit up. The builder must be very proud. I am too.
There goes the first lamp. And the next. Camille, they are queueing!
Lamp, lamp, lamp. Like someone running along with a match.
I always miss the very first lamp. Tonight I caught it. Victory.
Léo says the lamps light themselves. I am not correcting him.
Lamps on, glass full, child asleep. A perfect set.
The promenade is putting on its necklace. Very elegant.
The sun is touching the sea. Shh, Camille. Let it concentrate.
The sun is going into the sea like a coin into a fountain.
The bay just turned the colour of my wine. Coincidence? No.
I know one constellation. I make it up fresh each night.
Dancing beside the moon. It has the better spot, but fine.
Walking home with the moon. It keeps exactly my pace.
{name} is home. I would wave, but my hands are busy waltzing.
Bonne nuit, {name}. The window says it for you.
{name}'s light just went out. Sensible. I am following soon.
Bong. Bong. Six. My evening begins at once. Very punctual.
String lights, first song. Somebody has to begin. Not me. Yet.
The first note! Camille, this is our song. They all are.
So many people watching the sun. It must feel a little shy.
Hold on, {name} is waving. I am waving back. Professionally.
Bon appétit, {name}! Try the tarte. I did. Twice.
Inès again! She has done more laps than I have done steps.
Inès runs, I stroll. Together, a very average speed.
Biscuit trotted by with great purpose. Yusuf, with less.
Léo, slow down! Do as I do. Watch me. Very slow.
Asgeir! God morgen! ... It is evening. I only know the one.
There goes Asgeir to the post office. A man with a route.
The gull sounded hungry. I ordered more bread. Solidarity.
The gull laughed. I had not even told my joke yet.
Léo, wet shoes stay on the step, not in the house! Mostly.
Postcards of this very promenade. I am in none of them. Yet.
A kiosk orange, peeled in one long spiral. Bravo, me.
The post office does email for AI agents. I do postcards.
The post office is open all night. Tonight, so am I.
Its sign glows all night. Someone is always writing to someone.
Léo asked me for a noun. I said baguette. He sighed.
One MCP URL, every tool. One baguette, every meal. Same idea.
Lights on in the workshop. I wave. I am a supporter.
The library's lamp is still on. As if someone left a thought.
I tiptoe past the library. It is closed, but still. Manners.
The sea is wearing gold. Camille, it matches your earrings.
